question: For a fixed-pitch propeller at constant rpm, reducing forward speed:

options.text: Decreases the blade angle of attack
Increases the blade angle of attack

explanation: Lower V → smaller φ → larger α = β − φ.

question: Geometric pitch is:

options.text: The blade chord, measured along the line of the blade from the hub out to the tip of each blade at its widest point
The distance a blade element would advance in one revolution moving along its chord line: 2πr·tan β

explanation: Effective pitch (actual advance, V/n) is less than geometric pitch; the difference is slip.

question: Propeller slip is:

options.text: Tip speed minus TAS, which gives the speed of the blade through the air at the tip only
Blade angle minus helix angle in metres
Geometric pitch minus effective pitch (actual advance per revolution)

explanation: Slip reflects the blade's angle of attack; zero slip means zero α and zero thrust.

question: Propeller efficiency η = T·V/P. With T = 3,000 N at 60 m/s and shaft power 225 kW, η is:
Advance ratio J = V/(n·D). At 60 m/s, 40 rev/s, D = 2 m, J is:
Efficiency of a fixed-pitch propeller as a function of advance ratio:

options.text: Peaks at one J and falls on either side
Is constant across the whole range of advance ratios for any fixed-pitch design

explanation: At low J the blades work at high α (drag losses); at high J α falls toward zero thrust. Only one J (one speed at a given rpm) is optimum.

question: Propeller efficiency at zero forward speed (static) is:

options.text: Maximum, since the blades are then meeting the air at their most efficient angle
Zero, although thrust is at or near its maximum

explanation: η = T·V/P = 0 at V = 0: no thrust power is produced, even though thrust is large.

question: Maximum practical propeller efficiency is typically about:
explanation: Profile drag, tip losses, swirl in the slipstream and, at high speed, compressibility keep η below the ideal value.

question: A fixed-pitch propeller designed for cruise (coarse) compared with one designed for climb (fine):

options.text: Is identical, since the blade angle is the only variable that changes the propeller's output
Gives better cruise efficiency but lower take-off rpm and static thrust

explanation: Coarse blades at low V operate at high α (near stall) and absorb power at lower rpm, reducing engine power and thrust.

question: With a fixed-pitch propeller, increasing airspeed in a dive at constant throttle causes:

options.text: Rpm to increase (risk of overspeed), as blade α and torque fall
Rpm to decrease, as the blades stall at the higher airspeed and the propeller slows down

explanation: Lower α reduces absorbed torque; the engine accelerates the propeller.

question: A fine-pitch fixed propeller in cruise:

options.text: Is ideal for cruise, since the low blade angle gives the best efficiency at every speed
Operates at low α and high rpm, risking engine overspeed and poor efficiency

explanation: It is optimised for low speed; at high V the helix angle approaches the blade angle.

question: A constant-speed propeller maintains rpm by:

options.text: Varying mixture, which changes the fuel flow and so holds the engine speed constant
A governor adjusting blade angle to vary absorbed torque

explanation: Flyweights sense rpm; oil pressure (or springs/counterweights) change blade angle.

question: With a constant-speed propeller, increasing TAS at constant power and rpm causes the governor to:

options.text: Feather the propeller, since this is the normal response to any increase in airspeed
Increase the blade angle (coarser) to keep α and torque roughly constant

explanation: Higher V increases φ; β increases to maintain α = β − φ and absorbed torque.

question: With a constant-speed propeller, opening the throttle at constant rpm setting results in:

options.text: Higher rpm, because the throttle opening raises the engine speed at which the blades stop
A coarser blade angle to absorb the extra power at the same rpm

explanation: More engine torque would accelerate the propeller; the governor increases β to absorb it.

question: In a glide with throttle closed, a constant-speed propeller:

options.text: Moves to the fine-pitch stop; rpm then falls as power is insufficient
Goes coarse, which lets the propeller windmill and keeps the engine turning at a steady rate

explanation: The governor fines the blades to hold rpm until the fine stop is reached; then rpm decays and the windmilling propeller may produce drag.

question: For take-off, a constant-speed propeller is set to:

options.text: Reverse, which lets the engine develop full power at low forward speed in the take-off roll
Fine pitch / maximum rpm, allowing the engine to develop full power at low forward speed

explanation: Low blade angle at low V keeps blades unstalled and lets the engine reach rated rpm.

question: The advantage of a constant-speed propeller over a fixed-pitch propeller is:

options.text: Near-optimum blade angle of attack (and efficiency) over a wide speed range
Simplicity, since a fixed-pitch propeller has fewer moving parts and needs no governor at all

explanation: It avoids the single-optimum limitation of a fixed blade angle.

question: If oil pressure to a single-acting propeller that uses oil to increase pitch fails, the blades typically move:

options.text: To feather, since the springs and the oil pressure both move the blades to the feathered position
Toward fine pitch (high rpm), driven by centrifugal twisting moment and springs

explanation: With oil only able to coarsen the blades, losing it leaves the fine-pitch forces unopposed. Twin-engine designs reverse the arrangement: oil fines the blades and counterweights/springs drive them coarse or to feather on failure.

question: A feathered propeller has its blades:

options.text: At maximum rpm, so that the propeller is driven by the airflow at full speed and keeps the engine turning in the cruise
At about 90° to the plane of rotation, edge-on to the airflow, minimising drag and stopping rotation

explanation: Feathering removes windmilling drag after engine failure, improving single-engine performance and control.

question: A windmilling propeller produces:

options.text: Lift, since a windmilling propeller is driven by the airflow and so produces an upward force on the engine nacelle
Drag (negative thrust), being driven by the airflow at negative α

explanation: The relative flow strikes the blade's front face; the propeller extracts energy from the air to turn the engine.

question: Windmilling drag of a fine-pitch propeller compared with a feathered propeller is:
explanation: The disc of a windmilling fine-pitch propeller behaves like a large drag plate; feathering can reduce the drag several-fold.

question: Reverse pitch is used:

options.text: To feather, since reverse pitch is the same setting as the feathered position of the blades
On the ground after landing to produce reverse thrust for deceleration

explanation: A negative blade angle directs the slipstream forward.

question: The beta range on a turboprop refers to:

options.text: Direct pilot control of blade angle (ground operations, reverse) rather than governed constant-speed operation
Maximum cruise, since the beta range is the setting used to hold the propeller at its most efficient speed in flight

explanation: Power lever positions below flight idle select blade angle directly.

question: Selecting ground fine or reverse in flight is dangerous because:

options.text: The large drag and loss of lift over the wing behind the propeller can cause loss of control
It has no effect on the aircraft, since the propeller only produces thrust and no drag in any condition

explanation: Very low blade angles at flight speeds produce huge drag and disturbed flow; systems lock these ranges out in flight.

question: High tip Mach numbers are avoided because:

options.text: Shock formation at the tips reduces efficiency and increases noise
They reduce noise in the cabin, since the tip speed lowers the level of sound heard by the crew
They reduce thrust only at low speed

explanation: Compressibility losses rise steeply above tip M ≈ 0.85–0.9.

question: Reduction gearboxes are fitted between turbine engines and propellers because:

options.text: They reduce weight of the engine, which is the main reason the gearbox is fitted to any turboprop
Turbine shaft speeds would give supersonic propeller tips

explanation: Propeller rpm must be limited to keep the helical tip Mach number acceptable.

question: Propeller efficiency falls at high cruise speeds mainly because:

options.text: Helical tip Mach number rises toward sonic
Thrust rises, so the propeller must turn faster and the tips reach sonic speed at the same time

explanation: This limits conventional propeller aircraft to about M 0.6–0.7.

question: A propeller rotating clockwise when viewed from behind produces a torque reaction that:

options.text: Rolls the aircraft to the left (anticlockwise)
Yaws it right, since the torque reaction acts about the vertical axis of the aircraft in every case

explanation: Newton's third law: the airframe reacts opposite to propeller rotation.

question: During the take-off roll, torque reaction (clockwise propeller from behind) also causes a yaw to the left because:

options.text: Thrust is asymmetric, because the propeller's slipstream pushes harder on the left side of the fuselage
It loads the left main wheel more, increasing its rolling friction

explanation: Rolling moment transfers weight to the left wheel; increased drag on that side yaws the nose left.

question: The spiral slipstream of a clockwise propeller (from behind) strikes the fin:

options.text: On its left side, yawing the aircraft to the left
Symmetrically on both sides, so no side force reaches the fin
On its right side, yawing right

explanation: The slipstream rotates with the propeller and meets the fin from the left below it.

question: Asymmetric blade effect (P-factor) at high angle of attack, clockwise propeller from behind:

options.text: Gives more thrust from the descending (right) blade, yawing left
Gives more thrust from the ascending blade, yawing right
Produces no yaw at any angle of attack, since both blades share equal thrust

explanation: Inclined disc: the descending blade meets the air at higher α and speed.

question: Gyroscopic precession: a force applied to a spinning propeller disc takes effect:

options.text: 180° later, opposite to the direction of rotation
90° later in the direction of rotation

explanation: The angular momentum vector turns toward the applied torque vector.

question: Raising the tail of a tailwheel aircraft on take-off (clockwise propeller from behind) produces, through precession:
explanation: Pitching nose-down tilts the disc; the resulting precession moment yaws the nose left for this rotation direction.

question: Counter-rotating propellers on a twin (opposite rotation on each side) remove:

options.text: All drag from the propellers, which adds to the total drag of the twin at all speeds
The critical-engine asymmetry and cancel net torque and P-factor effects

explanation: Each side's effects mirror the other; engine failure on either side gives the same yawing moment.

question: Contra-rotating propellers (two coaxial propellers turning opposite ways) mainly:

options.text: Reduce thrust, since the second propeller always takes thrust away from the first
Recover slipstream swirl energy and cancel torque
Remove the need for a gearbox

explanation: The rear propeller removes the swirl left by the front one, improving efficiency.

question: All four propeller effects in a single-engine aircraft with a clockwise propeller (from behind) at high power and low speed tend to:

options.text: Yaw it right, requiring left rudder, because the torque acts in the opposite sense
Yaw the aircraft to the left, requiring right rudder

explanation: Torque (via wheel friction), slipstream, asymmetric blade effect and, when pitching down, precession all act to the left.

question: At constant shaft power 200 kW and η = 0.8, thrust at 50 m/s and 100 m/s is:
explanation: T = η·P/V: 160,000/50 = 3,200 N; 160,000/100 = 1,600 N. Propeller thrust falls with speed at constant power.

question: Power available from a propeller aircraft is approximately:

options.text: Zero at cruise, since the propeller stops delivering power once the aircraft levels off
Constant with speed (η·P), so thrust available falls with speed

explanation: Unlike a jet (roughly constant thrust), a propeller converts roughly constant engine power.

question: Best rate of climb for a propeller aircraft occurs near the minimum-power speed because:

options.text: Power available is roughly constant, so maximum excess power coincides with minimum power required
Drag is minimum there, so the aircraft reaches its best climb rate with the least drag and the most thrust at the same speed

explanation: ROC = (P_a − P_r)/W; with P_a flat, the maximum is where P_r is least.

question: A normally aspirated piston engine's power at altitude falls roughly in proportion to:
explanation: Mass flow of air per cycle falls with ρ; turbocharging restores sea-level manifold pressure to a critical altitude.

question: Propeller thrust at low speed is highest with:

options.text: Reverse pitch, which gives maximum thrust

explanation: Fine blades at low V avoid stall and allow full engine power.

question: Increasing propeller diameter at constant power:

options.text: Has no effect on the ideal efficiency, since a larger disc only changes the noise and nothing else
Improves ideal efficiency but raises tip speed and needs more ground clearance

explanation: A larger disc accelerates more air more gently; tip Mach and clearance limit diameter.

question: A propeller slipstream over the wing root and tail affects the aircraft by:

options.text: Increasing local dynamic pressure, raising lift behind the propeller and tail effectiveness at high power
Reducing lift over the wing root and tail at all power settings, since the slipstream always removes dynamic pressure from both

explanation: Power-on stall speeds are lower and elevator/rudder authority improves at high power and low speed.

question: Propeller-induced stall-speed reduction at high power arises from:

options.text: The thrust component supporting weight and the slipstream raising local q over the wing
Lower CLmax, because the slipstream reduces the local lift coefficient over the wing root at every power setting

explanation: L + T sin α = W and higher local dynamic pressure behind the disc.

question: For a constant-speed propeller in climb (low V, high power), the blade angle compared with cruise is:
explanation: Lower V gives lower φ; the governor reduces β to keep α suitable.

question: Thrust horsepower (thrust power) is:

options.text: Thrust × rpm, which gives the power delivered at the shaft

explanation: P_thrust = T·V; efficiency relates it to shaft power.

question: Governor overspeed protection moves the blades:

options.text: Coarser, to absorb more torque and reduce rpm
Finer, so that the blades absorb less torque and the engine speed is held steady

explanation: Increasing α and torque decelerates the propeller.

question: Auto-feather systems on twin turboprops:

options.text: Unfeather in cruise, so that the failed engine's propeller is restored to service whenever the aircraft levels off after take-off
Feather the failed engine's propeller automatically when torque drops below a threshold during take-off

explanation: Rapid feathering removes windmilling drag during the critical take-off phase.

question: Negative torque sensing on a turboprop:

options.text: Reverses pitch, which means the blades are driven to the reverse stop when the torque is negative in flight
Drives the blades toward coarse/feather when the propeller starts driving the engine

explanation: It limits windmilling drag after power loss before full feathering.

question: Gyroscopic effects are largest when:

options.text: Pitch or yaw rates are high and propeller rpm and inertia are large
The propeller is feathered, which removes the gyroscopic effect from every manoeuvre flown afterward
Speed is high but rates zero

explanation: Precession moment = I·ω_prop·Ω (Ω = aircraft rotation rate).

question: A pusher propeller behind the wing compared with a tractor:

options.text: Works in the disturbed wake of the airframe and gives less slipstream over the wing and tail
Eliminates P-factor, since the disturbed wake of the airframe cancels the asymmetric blade effect entirely

explanation: The inflow is non-uniform; propeller effects on tail authority are smaller.

question: In cruise, selecting lower rpm on a constant-speed propeller at the same power:

options.text: Reduces power, which lets the blades run at a lower speed and so the propeller produces less thrust
Increases blade angle and often improves efficiency (lower tip speed)

explanation: The governor holds the new rpm with coarser blades; manifold pressure increases to keep power.

question: A clockwise propeller (from behind) aircraft in a steep climb at low speed needs right rudder mainly because of:

options.text: Weight, because the steep climb puts the aircraft's full weight on the propeller

explanation: Airborne, wheel friction is absent; high α increases P-factor and high power strengthens the slipstream.

question: A propeller aircraft cruising at the minimum-drag speed achieves:

options.text: Maximum speed, since the minimum-drag speed is the highest speed the aircraft can attain in cruise
Maximum range (at constant η and specific fuel consumption)

explanation: Fuel flow ∝ power = D·V, so distance per unit fuel ∝ 1/D.
